newsitem.title: UK: Big Euro central bank gold sales unlikely - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Big Euro central bank gold sales unlikely - analyst.

text.p: Market fears that European countries will sell gold reserves to reduce their national debt levels are largely unsubstantiated, brokers T. Hoare and Company said in a report.

"In the vast majority of cases, the size of gold sales necessary to reduce the budget deficit to the required level is way too high, and generally considerably exceeds the amount of gold that any of these countries actually hold," wrote the report's author, analyst Rhona O'Connell.
"The Scandinavians would have to sell between five and 10 times what they actually own," she said.

The price of gold dived about $5.00 last week, partly on market concerns that European central banks were planning to sell some of their gold reserves to bring budget deficits in line with European Monetary Union (EMU) requirements.
But the only countries for which gold sales would be viable would be the Netherlands, Greece, Portugal and France, the report said.
The Netherlands, however, was already very close to meeting the EMU rules, it added.

France would be the only country that would retain an acceptable amount of gold in its foreign exchange reserves if it were to sell enough to reduce its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product, as required by EMU.

"This would reduce French gold, as a percentage of total foreign exchange, to 23 percent...assuming that the price did not respond -- which of course it would and the exercise would become self-defeating," the report said.
Other European countries which needed to bring their deficit down to the three percent level would have to sell more than they owned, it added.
"The conclusion to be drawn...is that in most cases gold sales would be more or less irrelevant in the greater scheme of things since there is not enough there in the first place," the report said.
However, if those countries that could sell gold in order to join the EMU did so, the amount involved would be around 2,000 tonnes, the report said.
